prelimsCapsule.coreConceptSummary: Development funding in India encompasses the multi-tiered financial architecture—ranging from Union budgetary allocations, Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS), Finance Commission transfers, and institutional credit to external development assistance—directed toward socio-economic transformation.
highYieldFacts: Fact 1: Article 275 and Article 282 of the Constitution govern grants-in-aid by the Union to the States for developmental purposes.
Fact 2: The Fifteenth Finance Commission recommended a vertical devolution of 41% of the divisible pool of central taxes to states for the period 2021-26.
Fact 3: Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) are categorized into Core schemes (with fixed central-state sharing patterns like 60:40 or 90:10 for North-Eastern states) and Core of the Core schemes.
Fact 4: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) administers the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) to finance ongoing rural infrastructure projects.
Fact 5: Capital expenditure (Capex) has been prioritized in recent Union Budgets through the Scheme for Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment, providing 50-year interest-free loans.
trapsAndElimination: Trap 1: Confusing Finance Commission grants (Article 275, statutory, recommended by a constitutional body) with discretionary grants under Article 282.
Trap 2: Assuming all Centrally Sponsored Schemes are fully funded by the Union government; most involve mandatory state co-financing ranging from 10% to 50%.
keyArticlesOrStatutes: Article 268-281 (Financial Relations between the Union and the States)

mainsFramework.inDepthTheoryHtml:
Evolution of Development Funding Architecture in India

The architecture of development funding in India has undergone profound shifts, evolving from centralized, plan-based resource allocation managed by the erstwhile Planning Commission to a cooperative and competitive federal model anchored by NITI Aayog, the Finance Commission, and targeted fiscal transfers. Effective development funding is critical not only for macroeconomic stability but also for bridging regional disparities and achieving inclusive growth aligned with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Mechanisms and Channels of Development Financing

Developmental expenditure flows through multiple distinct channels:

  • Tax Devolution: Unconditional transfers based on Finance Commission formulas, providing untied funds for states to prioritize localized developmental needs.
  • Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS): Conditional grants aimed at achieving national socio-economic priorities in health, education, and sanitation.
  • Extra-Budgetary Resources (EBR) and Institutional Financing: Leveraging institutions like NABARD, SIDBI, and multi-lateral development banks (World Bank, ADB) to fund infrastructure.
  • Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) and Viability Gap Funding (VGF): Crowding in private capital for capital-intensive public infrastructure projects.

Structural Bottlenecks and Governance Challenges

Despite reforms, development funding suffers from structural bottlenecks. Delays in fund transfers from the state treasury to implementing agencies, high conditionalities restricting operational flexibility, and low capital expenditure realization at sub-national levels impede optimal outcomes. Furthermore, vertical and horizontal fiscal imbalances exacerbate regional inequalities, as economically backward states often struggle with low own-source revenue generation.

dimensions.constitutional_or_legal: Interplay between Article 280 (Finance Commission) and Article 282 (Discretionary Grants), and fiscal federalism tensions over cess and surcharges which are excluded from the divisible pool.
dimensions.socio_economic: Targeting bottom-of-the-pyramid populations through welfare funding, addressing multidimensional poverty, and ensuring gender and social inclusion budgeting.
dimensions.administrative_governance: Implementation hurdles, treasury single account (TSA) system efficiency, bureaucratic delays, and tracking fund utilization via Public Financial Management System (PFMS).
dimensions.international_or_comparative: Adherence to international climate finance commitments, utilization of Green Bonds, and benchmarking against global sub-national fiscal decentralization standards.

prelims.question: Which of the following is/are among the erstwhile Planning Commission’s indicators for determining the backwardness of a State for development grants? (Consider standard historical context)
prelims.explanation: Backwardness criteria traditionally involved multi-dimensional indices including poverty ratios, per capita income, and infrastructure deficits rather than simplistic single-metric indicators.

modelMainsQA.question: Analyze the changing dynamics of development funding in India. How do conditional grants and fiscal centralization impact cooperative federalism and grassroots development? (250 Words, 15 Marks)

approach.intro: Define development funding in the context of Indian fiscal federalism, highlighting the transition from the plan era to contemporary cooperative/competitive federalism.
approach.body: Examine the role of statutory vs. conditional grants (CSS), the impact of rising cesses/surcharges on divisible pool devolution, and how these funding mechanisms affect state autonomy and grassroots implementation.
approach.conclusion: Suggest pathways for strengthening sub-national fiscal capacity, rationalizing CSS, and enhancing untied resource transfers to local bodies.

modelMainsQA.modelAnswerHtml:
Introduction

Development funding in India operates at the intersection of constitutional fiscal federalism and pragmatic socio-economic planning. With the dissolution of the Planning Commission and the enhanced recommendations of the Finance Commissions, the funding architecture has shifted toward greater untied devolution, balanced by conditional Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) designed to achieve national development targets.

Changing Dynamics and Fiscal Centralization

  • Erosion of Divisible Pool: A notable surge in the reliance on cesses and surcharges by the Union government—which are excluded from the divisible pool shared with states—has curtailed the absolute volume of statutory resources available to states.
  • Proliferation of Conditional Grants: While CSS ensure uniform focus on national priorities like health and education, rigid conditionalities often undermine local flexibility and mismatch regional needs.
  • Sub-National Fiscal Stress: States bear the principal responsibility for social sector spending (health, education, police) but command limited elastic tax handles post-GST, leading to heavy dependence on central transfers.

Impact on Cooperative Federalism and Grassroots Development

  • Asymmetry in Autonomy: Heavy reliance on conditional matching grants forces states to reallocate scarce resources toward central schemes, compromising state-specific developmental priorities.
  • Local Body Starvation: Despite Constitutional mandates (73rd and 74th Amendments), Panchayats and Urban Local Bodies remain fiscally anemic, relying heavily on tied grants rather than robust own-source revenue (property taxes, user charges).

Way Forward

Strengthening India's development funding requires rationalizing Centrally Sponsored Schemes into broad thematic envelopes, restricting cesses/surcharges to maintain buoyancy in the divisible pool, and empowering State Finance Commissions to enhance the fiscal autonomy of third-tier governance institutions in alignment with SDG localization.

practiceMCQs.question: Consider the following statements regarding development funding in India: 1. Grants given under Article 282 of the Constitution are recommended by the Finance Commission. 2. Cesses and surcharges levied by the Union are part of the divisible pool of taxes shared with states.
practiceMCQs.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect because Article 282 deals with discretionary grants made by the Union or a State for any public purpose, independent of Finance Commission recommendations (which fall under Article 275). Statement 2 is incorrect because cesses and surcharges are specifically excluded from the divisible pool of taxes shared with states under Article 270.

practiceMCQs.question: Which of the following bodies primarily administers the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF)?
options: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD)
practiceMCQs.answer: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD)
practiceMCQs.explanation: RIDF was instituted in NABARD by the RBI in 1995-96 out of shortfall in priority sector lending by commercial banks, with the objective of giving low-cost fund support to state governments to complete ongoing rural infrastructure projects.
